english: I'm jealous / I envy you (the nice kind)
usage: Polite; the everyday way to say you wish you had what someone has
Half-to-yourself exclamation, very common out loud
examples: 와, 부러워요!
Wow, I'm so jealous!
A warm reaction to someone's good news; 와 adds delight
휴가 간다고요? 진짜 부러워요.
You're going on vacation? I'm really jealous.
진짜 ('really') intensifies the friendly envy
집이 회사랑 가깝다니 너무 부러워요. 저는 한 시간 걸려요.
Your home is so close to work — I'm super jealous. Mine takes an hour.
Adding your own situation makes it sound sincere, not bitter
nuance: 부러워요 comes from the adjective 부럽다 ('to be envious'), and it is the GOOD, warm kind of envy — 'lucky you, I wish that were me.' Koreans say it constantly as a friendly compliment when you hear someone's nice news: a trip, a new phone, a close commute. It is NOT bitter or hostile. The phrase to keep far away from it is 질투 / 질투하다 ('jealousy'), which is the dark, possessive jealousy of a romantic rival or someone who resents your success — calling a friend's good news 질투나요 sounds creepy or resentful, so use 부러워요 for the everyday 'I envy you.' Register: 부러워요 is polite, 부러워 is 반말, and Koreans love the bare exclamation 부럽다 muttered out loud even to elders as a soft 'ahh, lucky.' The number-one English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the direction: you do NOT say 당신을 부러워요 ('I envy YOU' with an object) — the natural pattern marks what is envied with 이/가, so the bag you covet is 가방이 부러워요 ('I envy [your] bag'), the person/their situation is 네가 부러워, or, most often, you just say 부러워요 about the whole thing. A real trap is mixing up 부럽다 ('envious') with the look-alike 부끄럽다 ('shy/embarrassed') — they share 부 but mean opposite-feeling things; 'I'm jealous' is 부러워요, not 부끄러워요. To name what you envy, use 이/가: 네 휴가가 부러워.

usage: Polite-casual; about a situation, not usually said TO the person
반말, to a friend or muttered to yourself
-아 죽겠어요 ('to death') maxes out the frustration
네요 softens it to a shared grumble
examples: 아, 진짜 짜증나.
Ugh, this is so annoying.
Muttered to yourself or a close friend; 아 vents it
버스가 또 안 와요. 짜증나요.
The bus isn't coming again. So annoying.
About a frustrating situation, not a person
계속 같은 거 물어봐서 좀 짜증났어요.
They kept asking the same thing, so I got a bit irritated.
Past tense 짜증났어요 reports the irritation after the fact; 좀 softens it
nuance: 짜증나요 is from 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation arises'), the everyday word for the prickly, fed-up feeling when small things go wrong — the bus is late, the wifi drops, someone nags. It is honest and extremely common, but it is BLUNT and a little crude, so the safe zone is venting about a SITUATION to a friend or muttering to yourself; saying 짜증나요 straight to a person's face (especially a senior, a coworker, or staff) is rude and confrontational, like snapping 'you're pissing me off.' For a more controlled, polite 'that's a bit much,' Koreans soften with 좀 짜증나네요 or step up to the gentler-sounding 불편해요 ('it's uncomfortable/inconvenient') when complaining officially. The phrase people confuse it with is 화나요 ('I'm angry'): 화나다 is real, bigger anger, while 짜증나다 is petty irritation/annoyance — using 화나요 for a late bus overstates it, and using 짜증나요 about a serious betrayal understates it. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: it is the intransitive 짜증(이) 나다 ('irritation comes up'), so you say 짜증나요 (it arises in you), NOT 짜증해요 (not a word) and NOT 나를 짜증나요. If something/someone makes you annoyed, mark the cause with 때문에: 너 때문에 짜증나 ('I'm annoyed because of you') — still 반말-only and pointed.

usage: My heart's fluttering / I'm so excited
Polite; the giddy, hopeful kind of excitement
examples: 내일 여행 가요. 너무 설레요!
We travel tomorrow. I'm so giddy!
Sweet anticipation before something nice
첫 데이트라서 좀 설렜어요.
It was a first date, so my heart was fluttering a little.
Past 설렜어요 reports the flutter; classic for romance
새 학기라 설레면서도 좀 떨려요.
It's a new semester, so I'm excited but also a little nervous.
Pairing 설레다 (sweet) with 떨리다 (nervous) shows the warm-but-jittery mix
nuance: 설레요 comes from 설레다 ('to flutter, to feel one's heart race with sweet anticipation'). This is the warm, hopeful, butterflies-in-the-stomach excitement — before a trip, a date, a reunion, the first snow. It is gentle and romantic-leaning, and Koreans use it a lot in everyday life and all over song lyrics and dramas. The word to contrast it with is 떨리다 ('to tremble / be nervous'): 떨리다 is the JITTERY nerves before an exam or a speech (can be bad nerves), while 설레다 is the PLEASANT flutter you welcome — they overlap (a first date is both), but if you say 설레요 before a scary job interview it sounds odd, because 설레다 implies you're looking forward to it. Another near-word is 기대돼요 ('I'm looking forward to it'), which is cooler and more mental — 설레다 is the physical heart-flutter. Register: 설레요 polite, 설레 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation and spelling: the stem is 설레-, so it's 설레요 / 설렜어요 — NOT 설레여요 (a common wrong form) and NOT 설래요 (frequent misspelling). Also it's intransitive: 마음이 설레요 ('my heart flutters'), you don't 'do' 설레 to an object.

usage: It's so embarrassing / I feel awkward
-아 죽겠어요 maxes it for comic effect
examples: 아, 민망해.
Ugh, how embarrassing.
Muttered after a small social slip-up
사람들 앞에서 넘어져서 너무 민망했어요.
I fell in front of everyone, so I was so embarrassed.
Past 민망했어요 for the embarrassing moment
칭찬을 너무 많이 받으니까 좀 민망하네요.
Getting so much praise makes me a bit bashful.
민망하다 also covers the squirmy feeling of too much praise
nuance: 민망해요 (from 민망하다) is the squirmy, awkward embarrassment you feel after a small social misstep — you fell in public, you got caught, you received too much praise, an awkward silence dragged on. It's the 'oh no, this is so awkward, I want to shrink' feeling, and it's light/social, not deep shame. The big contrast is with 부끄럽다 and 창피하다: 부끄럽다 is shy/bashful (a blushing, modest shyness — also used for moral shame in writing), while 창피하다 is stronger, more 'humiliated / lost face' (you really screwed up publicly). Roughly: 민망하다 = awkward/uncomfortable embarrassment, 부끄럽다 = shy/blushing, 창피하다 = mortified/humiliated. Many learners pick one and overuse it; matching the strength matters. Register: 민망해요 polite, 민망해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 부끄러워요 for every kind of 'embarrassed' — but a fall in public or an awkward moment is more 민망해요 or 창피해요 than the shy 부끄러워요. Also it's an adjective describing your state: 민망해요 ('I feel awkward'), so don't say 민망당했어요 or attach an object — and don't confuse 민망하다 with the unrelated 미안하다 ('to be sorry'), which sound alike to beginners.

english: I feel proud and full (warm satisfaction)
usage: Exclamation to yourself after doing something well
examples: 다 끝냈어요. 뿌듯해요!
I finished it all. I feel so accomplished!
The warm glow after completing something
애가 상 받는 거 보니까 너무 뿌듯했어요.
Seeing my kid get an award, I felt so proud.
뿌듯하다 also covers warm pride watching someone you love succeed
한 달 동안 운동했더니 살이 빠져서 뿌듯해요.
After a month of exercise I lost weight, so I feel really fulfilled.
Pride in your own effort paying off; -았더니 shows the result of effort
nuance: 뿌듯해요 (from 뿌듯하다) is the warm, full, satisfied pride you feel inside after you (or someone you love) accomplished something — you finished a hard task, your kid did well, your effort paid off. The image is your chest swelling with quiet, happy fullness. It is INWARD and humble-feeling, which is why Koreans use it freely about themselves without sounding arrogant. The key contrast is with 자랑스럽다 ('to be proud (of)'): 자랑스럽다 is more outward/declarative pride you express ABOUT someone or something (아들이 자랑스러워요 'I'm proud of my son'), often spoken to or about others, while 뿌듯하다 describes the felt inner glow of satisfaction, usually about your own effort or a heartwarming moment. Saying 제가 자랑스러워요 ('I'm proud of myself') can sound boastful, but 뿌듯해요 sounds modest and relatable. Register: 뿌듯해요 polite, 뿌듯해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is using 자랑스럽다 for the personal warm-fuzzy feeling and accidentally sounding boastful, or trying to attach an object to 뿌듯하다 — it's an adjective for YOUR state (뿌듯해요), so you don't say 너를 뿌듯해요. Mark the cause with -아서/-니까: 끝내서 뿌듯해요 ('I feel fulfilled because I finished'). Don't confuse it with 만족하다 ('to be satisfied'), which is cooler and more evaluative.

Swapping in 만족해요 for the warm feeling.

english: I feel stifled / frustrated / boxed in
usage: It's driving me up the wall
examples: 방이 좁아서 좀 답답해요.
The room is small, so it feels a bit stifling.
Literal: a cramped, stuffy, closed-in physical feeling
말이 안 통해서 너무 답답해요.
We can't communicate, so it's so frustrating.
Emotional: blocked, can't get through to someone
엄마가 제 말은 안 듣고 자기 말만 해서 답답해 죽겠어요.
Mom won't listen to me and only talks, so it's driving me crazy.
The stuck, can't-make-them-understand frustration; -만 ('only') sharpens it
nuance: 답답해요 (from 답답하다) is a uniquely Korean feeling word covering a whole family of 'closed-in' sensations: physically stuffy/cramped (a tiny room, tight clothes, a stuffy chest), AND emotionally stifled/frustrated when you can't get through — communication isn't working, a slow person won't understand, you're stuck and powerless. The thread is 'blocked, can't breathe/can't get out.' This is different from 짜증나다 ('irritated') and 화나다 ('angry'): 짜증나다 is prickly annoyance at small things, 화나다 is outward anger, but 답답하다 is the INWARD, helpless, suffocating frustration of being stuck — often with no one to blame, just a blocked situation. There's no single English word, which is exactly why learners miss it: English speakers say 화나요 ('angry') when a Korean would say 답답해요 ('stifled/stuck'). A stronger sibling idiom is 속(이) 터지다 ('my insides burst') for extreme 답답함. Register: 답답해요 polite, 답답해 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) defaulting to 화나요/짜증나요 for this stuck feeling, and (2) the particle: the cause takes -아서/-때문에 (말이 안 통해서 답답해요), and the thing that's stifling can be the subject (가슴이 답답해요 'my chest feels tight'). Don't translate it as just 'frustrated (angry)' — it's the boxed-in, can't-get-through frustration.

english: I feel a little hurt / let down (by someone close)
usage: I feel a bit hurt / let down
Polite; quiet disappointment toward someone close
반말, to a close friend or family
네요 voices it gently, inviting acknowledgment
Why are you being so cold? (you're hurting me)
Said when someone's distance hurts you
examples: 연락 안 해서 좀 서운했어요.
You didn't text, so I felt a little hurt.
Past 서운했어요 for a quiet letdown by someone close
나만 빼고 갔다고? 좀 서운하다.
You went without me? That kind of stings.
반말 grumble of being left out by friends
벌써 가신다니 서운하네요. 더 계시지.

english: I feel relieved and unburdened (a weight lifted)
usage: Polite; the clean, cleared-out relief after a burden lifts
What a load off my chest
When the relief is mixed with a little sadness to let go
examples: 시험 끝났어요! 너무 후련해요.

오래 미루던 일을 끝내서 후련하면서도 좀 시원섭섭해요.

usage: Polite 네요 version said aloud to the person

hangul: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요
english: Please don't make this so frustrating / annoying
usage: 짜증 좀 안 나게 해 주세요

Polite-ish but pointed; use carefully, only when truly fed up
You're really getting on my nerves
Cleaner, less crude way to ask someone to stop

아, 진짜 사람 짜증 나게 하네.
Ugh, you're really getting on my nerves.

일부러 그러는 거예요? 짜증 나게.

-네 alone is 반말. Politely it's 설레네요. The -네요 adds 'oh, I notice...' warmth while staying polite.

english: I'm upset / it breaks my heart (a little)
usage: Polite; heartsore upset over something that went wrong
반말, to a friend or family
examples: 아끼던 컵이 깨져서 속상해요.
My favorite cup broke, so I'm upset.
Heartsore over a small loss; 아끼던 = 'that I treasured'
애가 아픈데 해 줄 게 없어서 너무 속상해요.
My child is sick and there's nothing I can do — it breaks my heart.
속상하다 for distressed, helpless heartache about a loved one
시험 망쳐서 속상하지? 괜찮아, 다음에 잘하면 돼.

Comforting someone; -지? checks their feeling gently

english: It's so vexing / I'm green with envy-and-frustration
usage: It's so vexing / it gets my goat
약(을) 올리다 = to taunt; the causative you'll hear a lot
Idiom: 'my stomach hurts' = resentful envy of others' luck
examples: 나만 안 됐다고? 아, 약 올라.
Only I didn't get it? Ugh, that's so vexing.
The teased, 'why-not-me' frustration; 나만 = 'only me'
동생이 자꾸 자랑해서 약 올라요.
My sibling keeps bragging, so it's getting on my nerves.
약 오르다 from someone flaunting/taunting
그만 약 올려요! 나도 갖고 싶단 말이에요.
Stop taunting me! I want one too, you know.
Causative 약 올리다 + -단 말이에요 ('I'm telling you')
nuance: 약 올라요 (from 약(이) 오르다, literally 'the 약/sap rises') is a vivid colloquial feeling: the prickly, vexed, 'argh, why not me / stop rubbing it in' frustration — a blend of envy and being teased/provoked. You feel 약 오르다 when others have what you can't, when someone flaunts or taunts you, when you're SO close but miss out. It's playful-to-genuinely-annoyed depending on tone, and very common among friends and siblings. The crucial pair is the causative 약(을) 올리다 ('to taunt, to rub it in, to get a rise out of someone'): 약 올리지 마 ('don't tease me') is everyday speech. Distinguish from plain 부럽다 (warm, clean envy 'lucky you') and 짜증나다 (general irritation): 약 오르다 specifically has that taunted/provoked, sour-grapes edge. english: Don't be so cold/distant — it hurts me
usage: Don't be so distant, it hurts
Polite but intimate; gently protests someone's coldness
Why are you being so cold?
Saying it that way hurts, you know
examples: 왜 이렇게 차가워요. 서운하게 그러지 마세요.
Why are you so cold? Don't be like that, it hurts.
Said to someone close who's being distant
가족끼린데 서운하게 왜 그래.
We're family — why are you being so cold?
끼리 ('among') appeals to closeness; gentle reproach
밥도 안 먹고 가면 제가 서운하죠. 조금만 더 있다 가세요.
If you leave without even eating, of course I'm hurt. Stay a little longer.
Warm 서운하죠 to make someone stay; -죠 = 'you know'
nuance: This entry teaches how to TELL someone they're hurting you — the relational repair move built on 서운하다. 서운하게 그러지 마세요 (lit. 'don't act in a way that makes me 서운') and 서운하게 왜 그래 ('why are you being so [cold/distant]?') are how Koreans gently push back when someone close is being cold, distant, or neglectful — WITHOUT escalating to a fight. The tone is intimate and a little vulnerable; you're saying 'you're hurting me because I care.' This only works with people you're close to (family, close friends, a partner); to a stranger or in formal settings it would be out of place. The near-synonym 섭섭하다 is fully interchangeable here (섭섭하게 왜 그러세요). Crucially, contrast this with the angry/blaming alternatives: 왜 이렇게 차갑게 굴어요? leans colder/accusatory, and 화내지 마 assumes anger — but the 서운하게 그러지 마 frame keeps it tender and reparative. The grammar lesson is the adverbial -게 + 그러다/그래 pattern: 서운하게 그러다 = 'to act in a 서운-causing way,' a super common construction (속상하게 하지 마, 섭섭하게 하지 마). The English-speaker pitfall is (1) not having this move at all — English speakers either bottle it up or escalate to 'I'm angry,' missing the gentle 서운 repair; (2) misusing -게: it attaches to the adjective stem (서운하게), and 그러지 마(세요) = 'don't do/act (that way)'; (3) confusing 그러다 ('to act/do so') with 그렇다 ('to be so'). Default register here is the intimate-polite 마세요 or 반말 왜 그래 — never formal.

Those assume anger and can start a fight. 서운하게 그러지 마 keeps it tender — 'you're hurting me because I care' — which repairs rather than escalates.

english: Now I finally feel some relief
usage: Polite; 이제야 ('only now, at last') + reflective 네요
What a total load off my chest
속이 다 ('insides, completely') for full release
십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요
Like a ten-year-old knot finally untied
examples: 다 말하고 나니까 이제야 좀 후련하네요.
Now that I've said it all, I finally feel some relief.
이제야 + -고 나니까 ('now that I've...') marks long-delayed release
그 사람한테 사과받고 나서 속이 다 후련했어요.
After getting an apology from them, what a load off my chest.
Deep 후련함 after a long grievance resolves
몇 년을 끌던 일이 끝나서, 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요.
The thing that dragged on for years is over — like a ten-year knot finally untied.
Pairs 후련함 with the vivid 묵은 체증 idiom
nuance: 이제야 좀 후련하네요 layers the time-nuance 이제야 ('only now, finally, at long last') and reflective -네요 onto 후련하다, producing the satisfying 'phew, AT LAST a weight is off me' you say when something you'd carried for a long time finally resolves. The real lessons here are (1) 이제야 vs. 이제: 이제 just means 'now,' but 이제야 adds 'only now / not until now,' implying it took too long — a small word that carries real feeling; and (2) the deep, idiomatic register of relief. For big, long-awaited release Koreans use vivid idioms: 속이 다 후련하다 ('my insides are completely cleared'), 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려가다 (lit. 'a ten-year-old case of indigestion finally goes down' = enormous pent-up relief), and 한(이) 풀리다 ('a deep grudge/regret is resolved'). Contrast 후련하다 with 시원하다 again (시원하다 is broader 'cool/refreshing'; 후련하다 is the emotional unburdening). Register: 후련하네요 polite; the -네요 ('oh, I notice') makes it sound like genuine, just-felt realization rather than a flat report. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) using flat 이제 and missing the 'finally/at last' weight that 이제야 adds; (2) defaulting to a generic 다행이에요 ('thank goodness') for this felt, bodily 'load off my chest' — they're different; (3) the -야 attaches to time/nouns to mean 'only then/only that' (이제야, 그제서야, 너야), so don't confuse it with the vocative 야 ('hey'). Match the size of relief to the phrase: small relief 후련해요, huge long-pent relief 십 년 묵은 체증이 내려간 것 같아요.

english: It's on my mind / it keeps bothering me
usage: It keeps bothering me / I can't stop thinking about it
Polite; something nags at your mind
Don't worry about it / never mind it
Telling someone to let it go (causative-ish 쓰다)
자꾸 ('repeatedly') + 네요 for a recurring nag
examples: 아까 그 말이 계속 신경 쓰여요.
What you said earlier keeps bothering me.
Something said that you can't stop turning over; 계속 = 'keep'
옆자리 사람이 자꾸 쳐다봐서 신경 쓰여요.
The person next to me keeps staring, so it's distracting/bothering me.
신경 쓰이다 for an external thing pulling at your attention
그건 제가 알아서 할게요. 신경 쓰지 마세요.
I'll handle that myself. Don't worry about it.
신경 쓰지 마세요 to release someone from concern
nuance: 신경 쓰여요 (from 신경(이) 쓰이다, lit. '나의 nerves get used/spent on it') is the everyday word for something that NAGS at your mind — you can't stop thinking about a comment, a staring stranger distracts you, a small unresolved thing pulls at your attention. It's mid-strength: more than nothing, less than full-blown 걱정 ('worry'). The crucial pair is the active vs. passive: 신경(을) 쓰다 = 'to pay attention to / care about / put effort into' (제가 신경 쓸게요 'I'll take care of it'), while 신경(이) 쓰이다 = the passive 'it bothers/preoccupies me (without my choosing).' Learners constantly mix these: 신경 써요 means 'I (actively) pay attention,' but 신경 쓰여요 means 'it nags at me.' The other essential phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't bother/worry about it'), an extremely common kindness. Distinguish from 걱정되다 ('I'm worried,' future-oriented anxiety about an outcome) and 거슬리다 ('it grates/irritates,' more negative/annoyed) — 신경 쓰이다 is the neutral 'it's on my mind/distracting me.' Register: 신경 쓰여요 polite, 신경 쓰여 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) confusing 쓰다 (active, 'spend nerves on = care/mind') with 쓰이다 (passive, 'be minded = it bothers me'); (2) literally translating 'bother' as 귀찮다 — but 귀찮다 is 'can't be bothered / it's a hassle (too lazy),' a different feeling; (3) marking it wrong — the thing that bothers you takes 이/가: 그 말이 신경 쓰여요, not 그 말을 신경 쓰여요.

english: It feels like too much / it puts pressure on me
usage: It feels like a lot / it's too much pressure
Polite; uneasy under expectation, attention, or generosity
Reassuring someone not to feel burdened
Isn't this putting pressure on you?
examples: 이렇게 비싼 선물은 좀 부담스러워요.

Uneasy at over-generosity; 좀 softens the refusal
다들 쳐다보니까 부담스러워요.
With everyone watching, I feel the pressure.
부담스럽다 under the weight of attention/expectation
편하게 생각하세요. 부담 갖지 마세요.
Take it easy — no pressure at all.

nuance: 부담스러워요 (from 부담스럽다, built on 부담 '負擔, a burden/load') is a socially essential Korean feeling with no neat English word: the uneasy 'this is too much for me' you feel under pressure, heavy expectation, intense attention, or someone's over-generosity. A too-expensive gift, a compliment that's over the top, everyone staring, a favor so big you'll feel indebted — all 부담스럽다. The thread is 'I feel weighed down / put on the spot, and I'd rather you dial it back.' It's polite and relational, often used to gently DECLINE or to soften: 부담스러우면 안 하셔도 돼요 ('if it's too much, you don't have to'). The key partner phrases are 부담(을) 주다 ('to pressure/burden someone') and 부담(을) 갖다 ('to feel pressured'), so 부담 갖지 마세요 ('don't feel pressured / no pressure') is a constant kindness, and 부담 주려는 건 아닌데 ('I don't mean to pressure you, but...') softens a request. Distinguish from 어렵다 (here 'someone feels intimidating/hard to be around,' e.g. a strict boss) and 무겁다 (literally 'heavy') — 부담스럽다 is specifically the felt social weight of expectation/obligation. Register: 부담스러워요 polite, 부담스러워 반말. The English-speaker pitfall is (1) having no word for it and instead bluntly refusing ('no, too expensive'), where a Korean softens with 부담스러워요 to decline graciously; (2) the -스럽다 adjective form — it's 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (irregular ㅂ), not 부담해요 or 부담있어요; (3) mixing up 부담 주다 ('to burden someone') with 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened') — 'you're pressuring me' is 부담스러워요 / 부담 주지 마세요, while 'I don't want to burden you' is 부담 드리고 싶지 않아요.

mistakes: Bluntly refusing instead of softening with 부담스러워요.
To decline a big gift/favor graciously, Koreans say 좀 부담스러워요 ('it's a bit much for me'). A flat 'no, too expensive' is harsher; 부담스럽다 keeps it polite and relational.
Saying 부담해요 or 부담있어요.
The adjective is 부담스럽다 → 부담스러워요 (ㅂ-irregular). There's no 부담하다 for this feeling, and 부담있어요 isn't natural. Use 부담스러워요.
Confusing 부담 주다 with 부담스럽다.
부담 주다 = 'to pressure/burden someone (else)'; 부담스럽다 = 'I feel pressured/burdened.' 'You're pressuring me' = 부담스러워요 / 부담 주지 마세요, not 부담스러워 주세요.
